concurrency_model: Training: at most one training job at a time (TrainService._check_no_concurrent_jobs under _start_lock against JobStore status); each job runs the pipeline on a daemon thread; cancellation is cooperative via CancellableJobRegistry + ExecutionContext.checkpoint() polled from _report/_on_iteration/check_cancelled; CatBoost GPU fit runs on a worker thread polling learn_error.tsv with a bounded abort-join (30s) and loud zombie logging. Model load cache (_mlflow_io._model_cache, _ModelCacheWithCascade over LRUCache, max 16): per-(run_id, artifact_path) reentrant I/O lock (WeakValueDictionary) provides single-flight download+load (avoids thundering herd, rename-over-open-file, and corrupt-retry-unlink races); disk-cache eviction guarded by a per-run in-use Counter so an active run dir is never rmtree'd; eviction cascades to invalidate _model_scorer feature-validation cache (also LRU max 16) outside the cache lock to avoid deadlock. Cache hit/miss counters under a dedicated stats lock. Feature-validation cache adds a non-locked single-entry last-entry fast path keyed on id(model)+contract+schema items. Deploy + contract caches are StatGatedCache (per-key single-flight, gated on mtime_ns+size). ScoringModel reuse pinned per-scorer under a lock for streaming chunk jobs. Temp-file cleanup uses a module lock + atexit + contextvar scope.
perf_characteristics: Designed for low peak memory on wide/large data: parquet staging at every stage with streaming bounded_sink, column projection pushed into scans (GLM reads only term cols; CatBoost reads features+target+weight+offset), float32 cast for CatBoost Pools, aggressive del+gc.collect()+_malloc_trim between stages, and a persistent RSS memory log (_mem_checkpoint). Scoring offers eager (single predict, one materialisation) vs batched (sink + 500k-row parquet iter_batches) paths chosen by caller, never auto-detected. Model loads cached in-memory (16) and on-disk (.cache/models, 50 run dirs, atomic move, ~30s+ saved vs Databricks re-download). Feature validation, contract reads, and deploy artifacts memoised on hot per-request/per-batch paths. Diagnostics partition read exactly once. SHAP subsamples to 1000 rows. Known cost: explainability and per-batch validation re-derive categorical sets; batched scoring writes a full intermediate parquet.
invariants: Cache key uniquely identifies model content: _model_cache_key=(source_type, resolved_run_id, version_or_artifact, task); a wrong key returns the wrong model. The fast-path key (version='') must agree with the resolved-path key for the same artifact.

Feature order is positional for CatBoost: categorical indices are positional, so _validate_features enforces the input schema presents model features in the SAME relative order as training; a reorder must raise, never silently mis-encode.

Per-flavor predict-frame contract: rustystats gets raw Polars, pyfunc gets named pandas with native dtypes (no preemptive float downcast), catboost gets float32 numerics + _MISSING_-filled pd.Categorical; unknown flavor must raise, never fall through to catboost/pyfunc shape.

Eager and batched scoring must produce identical predictions and identical proba semantics — both route shape reduction through _positive_class_proba_vector (1-D as-is, (n,1)->col0, (n,2)->col1, multiclass raises).

Row alignment is structural: eager scoring collects ONCE and attaches predictions to that same frame so an order-unstable upstream (group_by w/o maintain_order, unique, streaming join) cannot land predictions on wrong rows; categorical-domain validation runs on the same materialisation that is scored.

Feature contract hash = sha256 of canonical sort-keyed JSON of all fields except the hash; load_contract must reject a hash that disagrees with content. categorical_levels are explicit metadata, never inferred from rows; None is an explicit null level.

Train-vs-score drift fails loudly: assert_contracts_match raises FeatureMismatchError naming the offending field; deploy _assert_runtime_contract_matches rebuilds the contract from live schema before any model load.
Null-target rows must be removed before any trainer sees them; a temporal split with null dates must raise (no silent routing); split fractions validation_size+holdout_size<1.

Artifact disk-cache path never escapes cache_root: _validate_disk_cache_run_id + _validate_artifact_path + is_relative_to(cache_root) guard; run_id/artifact_path with sep/..\/NUL must raise. score_from_config config path must resolve within project root.

SHAP/contribution explanations must reconstruct the model prediction within tolerance (raw-formula space for CatBoost, accounting for Poisson/Tweedie exp link); a mismatch raises rather than presenting a wrong attribution. GLM inference stats are never fabricated (GLMInferenceUnavailableError).

config->TrainingJob kwargs is single-sourced (build_train_params/build_training_job_kwargs) so live training and exported scripts can never train different models; GLM keys merged for GLM only (CatBoost has no **kwargs).
Run-owned temp parquets (owns_tmp=True) are always cleaned on abort; caller-supplied parquet inputs are never deleted.
Optional diagnostics (SHAP/PDP/GLM) failures are recorded in diagnostics_errors and surfaced, never silently swallowed; mandatory steps (feature_importance, compute_metrics) propagate.

candidate_risks.concern: pyfunc/RustyStats models are logged with loader_module="haute._mlflow_io" (_mlflow_log.py:471-475) but _mlflow_io defines no module-level _load_pyfunc(path)/load_model symbol that MLflow's pyfunc loader-module contract requires (only _load_pyfunc_model(mlflow, run_id, artifact_path), a different signature). A consumer loading the logged model through mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(runs:/.../model) would hit AttributeError/contract failure; haute only works because it separately logs the native .rsglm via mlflow.log_artifact and loads that instead.
candidate_risks.why: Silent contract breakage: the MLflow artifact advertises a pyfunc flavor that cannot actually be loaded by standard MLflow tooling, and the ModelSignature attached to it is the documented drift-detection surface for deploy. External consumers or future code paths relying on pyfunc.load_model would fail or be misled.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Hidden until someone loads via the pyfunc flavor; native path masks it for the common case.

candidate_risks.concern: load_mlflow_model fast-path uses cache key with version='' for source_type=='run' (artifact known), while the resolved path builds the key with resolved_version. For source_type=='run' resolved_version stays '' so they match, but if a run-sourced load ever resolves a non-empty version, the fast-path PUT (version='') and the resolved GET (version set) would diverge and double-load / never hit. Also _model_cache is keyed by raw run_id on the fast path but resolved_run_id elsewhere; for 'run' these are equal, but registered models only ever take the slow path.
candidate_risks.why: Cache-key divergence silently defeats the cache (extra downloads) or, worse, could serve a stale entry if a run_id maps to different artifacts across versions. Numerical correctness is fine but performance/observability invariants degrade invisibly.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Current call paths keep the keys consistent; risk is latent if version semantics for run sources change.

candidate_risks.concern: CatBoostAlgorithm.predict (used for TRAINING-TIME metrics/diagnostics) returns predict_proba[:,1] for a CatBoostClassifier, whereas the SCORING path (ScoringModel.predict via score_frame) returns model.predict() (class label) and appends proba separately. So the y_pred used for training metrics (gini/auc/lorenz/residuals) is the positive-class probability, while scored output 'prediction' is the hard label. Whether this is intended differs by metric; residuals_histogram/actual_vs_predicted on a classification task would mix proba-as-prediction semantics.
candidate_risks.why: Train-time diagnostics and live scoring report different 'prediction' semantics for the same model; a reviewer auditing classification metrics could be misled, and residual-style diagnostics on probabilities vs labels are not obviously correct.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Classification is secondary to the pricing/regression focus, but silent semantic mismatch in reported metrics is a correctness-of-reporting issue.

candidate_risks.concern: _group_split/_group_mask hash groups with md5(seed:group) and take a fraction threshold; this gives no guarantee the realised validation fraction is close to validation_size (it is a Bernoulli draw per group), and the 'force at least one validation group' fallback only triggers when zero groups land in validation. Temporal mask sorts non-train rows by arg_sort of dates that may have ties; holdout assignment via slice of arg_sort is order-dependent on tie-breaking.
candidate_risks.why: Silent statistical bias: a user requesting 20% validation can get a wildly different split with skewed group sizes, affecting reported metrics and model selection without any error. Tie-handling in temporal holdout could be non-deterministic across Polars versions.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Behaviour is deterministic-by-seed and documented as hashing; bias is a known trade-off rather than a bug, but worth a numerical-stability audit.

candidate_risks.concern: _validate_features keys on (id(scoring_model), contract, schema items). id() is reused after an object is GC'd; the design relies on the _model_cache eviction cascade (_invalidate_feature_validation_cache_for) to drop entries when a ScoringModel leaves the cache. But ScoringModels created OUTSIDE _model_cache (e.g. _score_batched_unified builds a transient carrier ScoringModel, load_local_model in deploy, reuse_loaded_model pinned instances) are never registered in _model_cache, so their feature-validation entries are only protected by the contract component of the key against id-reuse — a different model with an identical feature contract and schema but different weights could collide on a reused id and return a stale (usable, missing) tuple.
candidate_risks.why: The cached value is only (usable_features, missing_features), which depends solely on names/contract/schema, so a collision returns a structurally-correct answer; the risk is subtle (entry never validates the NEW object) but currently appears benign because the cached result is content-equivalent. Still a shared-state correctness lead if the cached payload ever grows to include model-specific data.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Cached payload is name/schema-derived so a collision yields the same answer today; flagged because the id()-reuse + selective-cascade design is fragile to future changes.

candidate_risks.concern: GPU CatBoost fit runs on a daemon worker thread; on cancellation the helper joins up to 30s and, if still alive, logs and re-raises leaving train_dir on disk and the thread running. The fit thread holds the CatBoost model and the Pool; abandoning it leaks GPU/host memory and a train_dir, and a subsequent training job is blocked only by the single-job guard at the route layer (the abandoned thread could still be writing files).
candidate_risks.why: Concurrency/resource leak under cancellation: a cancelled GPU run can leave a live writer and temp dir; repeated cancels could accumulate zombie threads/dirs. Loudly logged but not recoverable in-process.
candidate_risks.why_severity: GPU path is opt-in, the abandon is bounded and logged, and the single-job lock limits accumulation; still an unbounded-resource lead under repeated cancellation.

candidate_risks.area: Batched scoring proba in zero-row / projection path
candidate_risks.concern: _batch_score_to_parquet decides can_predict_proba via _raw_model_supports_predict_proba but the empty-frame branch and the per-chunk write_projection branch both gate the proba column on slightly different conditions (want_proba + support vs proba_col present in chunk.columns). If the first batch lacks proba (model returns None at runtime despite advertising predict_proba) but later batches differ, the ParquetWriter schema is fixed from the first table and a later schema change would raise; conversely empty-input writes a Float64 proba column whose presence depends on can_predict_proba, which may not match a non-empty run.
candidate_risks.why: Schema drift between batches / between empty and non-empty inputs could either raise mid-write or produce outputs whose columns depend on row count — a subtle output-contract inconsistency feeding downstream pricing.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Requires a model whose predict_proba support varies at runtime; defensive but a real edge for custom pyfunc models.

candidate_risks.concern: coefficients_table/relativities have multi-level fallbacks (coef_table -> bse/tvalues/pvalues arrays -> raise) and _align_coefs_and_names prepends (Intercept) heuristically when len(coefs)>len(names). If RustyStats ever returns coefficients and names of equal length but mis-ordered, the intercept alignment and the per-index zip in relativities() could silently mislabel coefficients/relativities without tripping the length guard.
candidate_risks.why: Silent mislabeling of GLM relativities (the core actuarial output) would present wrong factor relativities as correct; only length mismatches are guarded, not ordering/identity.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Depends on RustyStats name/coef ordering contract; the explainability path independently re-checks additivity, but the diagnostics table does not.

candidate_risks.concern: _save_artifacts writes a per-model {name}.feature_contract.json but only WARNS (never rewrites/removes) a leftover shared feature_contract.json. If a deploy bundle or a feature_contract_path config still points at the legacy shared file, it silently describes whichever model trained last.
candidate_risks.why: A stale shared contract pointed at by older config silently validates against the wrong model's schema — drift detection would pass when it should fail. Mitigated by per-model naming + loud warning, but the old file is left in place.
candidate_risks.why_severity: Only bites pre-existing deployments using the legacy path; new paths are per-model.

region: Price optimisation (per-record gradient + ratebook coordinate descent; efficient frontier)
purpose: Constrained portfolio price-optimisation engine exposed as FastAPI endpoints. Given an optimiser node in a pipeline graph, it executes the upstream graph lazily to materialise a long-format scored DataFrame (one row per quote x scenario step), validates/projects it, builds a Rust QuoteGrid, and runs one of two solvers from the bundled `price_contour` library: (1) ONLINE mode = per-record Lagrangian dual decomposition (each quote independently picks the scenario step maximising obj + signed-lambda*constraint); (2) RATEBOOK mode = coordinate descent over rating-factor tables. It also computes the efficient frontier (sweep over constraint-threshold ranges), estimates achievable frontier ranges from the scenario envelope (auto-range), and supports apply/save/MLflow-log of solved lambdas/factor tables. Haute owns ALL orchestration, streaming/chunking, validation, artifact lifecycle, concurrency and result materialisation; the numerical kernels live in price_contour (Rust + thin Python).

Server-owned parquet artifacts (apply result, ratebook factors) must live under the resolved temp artifact root, use absolute paths, correct kind/version/format, the expected directory prefix and filename; path resolution must not escape the artifact root (_validate_server_owned_parquet_handle).

AUTO_RANGE projection subset invariant: auto_range_required_columns ⊆ solver_required_columns per node, so the opportunistic dataframe-execution cache warmed during auto-range can be reused (or correctly rejected) by a later solve without violating AUTO_RANGE's narrow-projection contract (_execute_pipeline comment, lines ~4199-4240).

Concurrency: only ONE blocking solve job may run at a time (estimate + auto-range are non-blocking); a graph/node single-flight key prevents concurrent setup for the same (graph_fingerprint,node); job-store updates are whole-dict atomic swaps so status pollers never see half-updated state.

Heavy-object lifecycle: solver/solve_result/quote_grid (+ratebook factor contexts/factors_df) are retained only for a bounded window after completion; apply/frontier/save/mlflow re-touch them via touch_heavy_objects and fail loudly (400) if already evicted — they are never fabricated.

Ratebook /apply is unsupported by contract: RatebookResult has no per-quote dataframe, so /apply is gated at the route (422) AND defended in depth before apply_from_grid, because apply_from_grid would silently ignore solved factor tables.

Apply neutral-miss policy: a ratebook factor level the solver never saw keeps factor 1.0 (onMissing=neutral, no defaultValue) but is LOUD — counted, logged, and flagged 'unseen' in the explainer; it never fails the whole apply.
None constraint thresholds are frontier-only markers: solve()/apply() reject them; frontier() requires a matching threshold_ranges entry per None constraint.

internal_dataflow: "IN: OptimiserSolveRequest{graph, node_id, source, streaming_chunk_size}. start() flattens the graph, finds the OPTIMISER node, reads node.data.config, validates config -> mode. A solve job is registered (single-flight on (graph_fingerprint,node_id)) BEFORE heavy work so long local runs stay pollable. Background setup thread: execute_lazy_graph runs the pipeline up to the optimiser's data_input (with an opportunistic optimiser_setup dataframe-execution cache request) -> lazy_outputs; _resolve_data_source picks the configured data_input (or sole parent); _validate_and_project does a single streaming pass to reject null quote_id + non-finite objective/constraint/scenario values, then projects+casts solver columns; for ratebook, _extract_factors sinks the banding source's projected factor columns to a parquet artifact (handle). scored_lf is sunk to a temp parquet and build_grid_from_parquet_chunked builds the QuoteGrid (chunk size from a byte-budget policy keyed off execution-profile memory). The grid (and ratebook factor contexts) hand off to a SOLVER background thread. ONLINE: OnlineOptimiser.solve -> solve_online_py / solve_from_grid_py (Lagrangian dual). RATEBOOK: build factor contexts (fingerprint-aligned), RatebookOptimiser.solve -> run_cd_pass_py (full CD pass in Rust). _finalize_solve_result builds the result dict (totals, baseline, lambdas, converged, scenario-value stats+histogram from optimal_scenario_value), OPTIONALLY computes the frontier inline if frontier_enabled, persists the apply-result + ratebook-factor artifacts behind handles, and atomically transitions the job to completed with heavy objects (solver, solve_result, quote_grid) retained for a bounded window. OUT: status endpoint returns the result summary + capped frontier payload + execution_metrics. FRONTIER recompute: re-touch solver+grid, enforce compute budget, solver.frontier(threshold_ranges,...), cap to FRONTIER_POINT_LIMIT, store points, invalidate stale per-point apply artifacts. FRONTIER-SELECT/APPLY: reconstruct a point's result dict from stored points (lambdas parsed from lambda_* fields); ratebook points are re-solved on demand (solver.solve with _constraints_override) and factor tables re-serialised; online apply points run apply_from_grid and persist a per-point artifact. AUTO-RANGE: reads quote_id+constraint columns; per quote independently chooses min/max scenario; reduced in bounded batches to per-quote extrema, hash-partitioned to disk buckets (so quotes split across read batches recombine), then bucket totals summed -> achievable (min,max) envelope per constraint. A streaming variant chunks BEFORE scenario expansion when a chunk-local plan can be proven. APPLY/SAVE/MLFLOW: build optimiser_result.json payload (lambdas, totals, constraints, factor tables for ratebook) and write to a sandbox-validated path or MLflow run."
concurrency_model: "Heavily concurrent and the dominant risk surface. Each solve/auto-range runs across two daemon threads (setup, then solver) plus the request thread. Shared state is a process-global in-memory JobStore (one singleton per 'optimiser' prefix). Writes go through atomic_update / atomic_update_if_heavy_present which build a NEW dict and swap it in under a _write_lock; readers (status polling) rely on CPython GIL atomicity of dict.__setitem__ to see either old or new, never partial. expected_status guards prevent a timeout/supersede from clobbering a completed result. Job admission/cancellation: ExecutionCancellationToken + CancellableJobRegistry (per-job 'latest' registration that supersedes older same-key jobs) for solve, auto-range and graph-node-setup, each polled via _raise_if_*_stopped at checkpoints between phases. A SingleFlightCoordinator on (GRAPH_NODE_SETUP, node_id, graph_fingerprint) serialises setup for the same graph/node; _check_no_concurrent_jobs rejects a second BLOCKING solve (estimate/auto-range are non-blocking). Heavy runtime objects (solver/solve_result/quote_grid/ratebook contexts) have a separate retention timer; after expiry they are stripped, and apply/frontier/save/mlflow re-acquire via touch_heavy_objects (failing 400 if gone). Background threads deliberately use direct store.jobs.get(...) in a few spots (e.g. _finalize_solve_result M6 comment) to avoid triggering eviction from the worker thread. Extensive artifact-orphan cleanup in finally/except blocks handles races where a job's atomic completion update is skipped (superseded) after artifacts were already written."
perf_characteristics: "Designed for large local datasets under bounded memory. Numerical kernels are Rust (solve_online_py / run_cd_pass_py) operating on f32 grids; the ratebook CD pass keeps residuals/multipliers Rust-side to avoid ~max_cd*n_factors*2 PyO3 round-trips of 100k-element buffers per solve. Grid/factor materialisation is parquet-sink + chunked-read with chunk size derived from a byte budget (target chunk bytes scaled from the execution profile's memory limit, clamped 16MiB..512MiB). Validation, estimate and auto-range are single streaming-aggregation passes with projection pushdown (estimate folds the null-quote_id check into the same group_by scan). Auto-range avoids a global per-quote table by hash-partitioning per-batch extrema to disk buckets then reducing per bucket; a streaming variant chunks before scenario expansion to cap peak rows when the suffix is provably chunk-local. Frontier is O(n_points_per_dim ** n_constraints) full solves; capped at 10000 grid points (compute budget) and 2000 returned points (response cap). Frontier warm-starting: ratebook uses nearest-neighbour visit order + linear lambda predictor-corrector; online ratio/unswept sweeps use sequential warm-start. Apply preview capped at 100 rows. Large apply/detail dataframes and ratebook factors are spilled to parquet artifacts behind handles rather than held in the (memory-resident) job dict."

complexity_hotspots.what: End-to-end solve setup orchestration with ~7 distinct terminal-failure exception arms (BackgroundJobStopped, HTTP 4xx/5xx, admission/memory, bounded-memory-unsupported, generic) each mapping to a different lifecycle transition + execution-metrics payload + artifact cleanup; the finally arm releases three registries + single-flight + orphan ratebook artifact.

Two ~250-line near-parallel auto-range drivers (standard vs pre-expansion streaming) with duplicated progress/cancellation/exception/lifecycle scaffolding; the streaming path threads a chunk plan, per-chunk validate+project, and a disk-bucket accumulator.
Hash-partitioned, disk-backed per-quote min/max aggregation with bucket combine/total expr sets; the numerical correctness of the achievable envelope depends on this recombination.

_canonical_ratebook_table_level / _serialise_ratebook_factor_table_rows: combinatorial candidate matching of solver-emitted level reprs against canonical count keys, with minimal-collapse winner selection and loud failure on ambiguity; subtle and correctness-critical for apply alignment.
Shared result finalisation with inline optional frontier compute, dual artifact persistence, atomic completion, and multi-branch orphan cleanup when the completion update is skipped.
Builds the dataframe-execution cache request including the AUTO_RANGE->solver column-superset merge that the cache-key reuse invariant depends on.

On-demand re-solve of a ratebook frontier point and online per-point apply-artifact materialisation, each with cached-result fast paths, heavy-object touch guards, atomic-if-heavy-present updates, and 409 races.

Decorates a Rust SolveResult to recompute actual ratios for ratio constraints, including a pure-Python per-iteration Lagrangian-argmax replay for history (route (b)); the most numerically subtle wrapper, with a special final-iteration alignment rule.
Predictor-corrector frontier sweep: NN ordering, linear lambda extrapolation along prev2->prev, unswept-axis handling, per-point constraint override, points re-sorted to cartesian order.

candidate_risks.concern: Auto-range silently DROPS entire read-batches whose quote_id column contains any null, then reports the dropped count only via a post-hoc null_quote_id_count check at finish().
candidate_risks.why: _ScenarioFrontierRangeAccumulator.add_batch returns early for the whole batch when null_count>0 (lines ~1462-1465), incrementing null_quote_id_count by the null count but excluding ALL rows in that batch (including non-null quotes) from bucket aggregation. finish() raises if null_quote_id_count>0, so behaviour is to fail — but if a future change makes that non-fatal, or if batching interacts with the streaming variant differently, non-null quotes in a tainted batch would be silently excluded from the min/max envelope. The fail-vs-include asymmetry is subtle and the dropped-rows accounting only covers the null rows, not the co-batched valid rows.

candidate_risks.concern: Canonical level resolution picks the candidate that collapses the FEWEST components and FAILS on ties; correctness of apply-time rate lookup hinges on the claim that ties are impossible for single-dtype frames.
candidate_risks.why: _canonical_ratebook_table_level builds float/verbatim candidate combinations per component and asserts the minimal-collapse winner is unique. If a real (e.g. mixed-dtype, or string column whose literal values look like collapsible floats such as '25.0' and '25' both present as counted levels) factor column reaches here, it raises ValueError mid-save and the whole solve result becomes unsaveable, OR—if counts were built from a different frame than the solver grouped on—could mis-map a level to the wrong canonical key and silently apply the wrong rate. The level_counts must describe exactly the solved frame; any divergence is a silent-correctness hazard.

candidate_risks.concern: Legacy frontier_min/frontier_max changed meaning: comment says they are 'no longer treated as a multiplier on baseline values' and are now absolute, applied to every constraint.
candidate_risks.why: _auto_frontier_ranges_from_config returns {cname:(frontier_min,frontier_max) for cname in constraints} — the SAME absolute range for every constraint. For multi-constraint configs with different scales (e.g. premium total vs loss-ratio), a single shared absolute (min,max) is almost certainly wrong for at least one axis, and the silent fallback (when frontier_ranges is absent but frontier_min/max present) could produce a misleading frontier rather than erroring. Worth auditing whether any saved configs still carry the legacy pair and what the frontend emits.

candidate_risks.concern: Opportunistic AUTO_RANGE cache warming advertises solver-required columns in the cache key while executing with the narrower auto-range projection demand; relies on the auto_range ⊆ solver subset invariant AND on a runtime seed-time column check to reject mismatches.
candidate_risks.why: If the subset invariant is ever violated (e.g. a future constraint/objective column added to auto-range but not solver projection, or a node that drops columns between the two profiles), a later solve could HIT a cache artifact that lacks solver columns, or reuse an artifact whose contents differ from what the solver needs. The code itself flags this as load-bearing (comment lines ~4199-4240). A subtle projection regression here would surface as wrong solver input or an opaque rebuild, not a clear error.

candidate_risks.concern: Background worker reads/writes job dict via a mix of atomic_update(expected_status=...) and direct store.jobs.get(...) (M6), and several apply/frontier paths do touch_heavy_objects -> require_completed_job -> read solver/grid as separate steps.
candidate_risks.why: Between touch_heavy_objects (which extends the retention window) and the subsequent require_completed_job + .get('solver'), the heavy-object timer or a concurrent clear_result_data/atomic completion could still race; the code mitigates with atomic_update_if_heavy_present and 409s, but the multi-step get patterns in _ratebook_runtime_state_or_raise and _materialise_frontier_point_apply are intricate and a missed re-check could surface a None solver as a 500 or, worse, operate on partially-cleared state. High-value area for a focused concurrency audit.

candidate_risks.concern: Frontier point lambdas are reconstructed by string-prefix parsing of lambda_* fields and constraint values from total_*/constraints/bare-name keys, with finite-float coercion; ratebook points are then RE-SOLVED rather than using stored optima.
candidate_risks.why: _frontier_point_lambdas/_frontier_point_constraint_value/_frontier_point_constraints_override pull values from heterogeneous dict shapes. A frontier point whose stored schema differs slightly (e.g. a constraint named 'total_x' colliding with the total_ prefix convention, or a lambda key collision) could parse the wrong value. For ratebook, _materialise_ratebook_frontier_point re-runs solver.solve with _constraints_override derived from threshold_* fields — so the displayed/saved factor tables depend on re-solving converging to the same point the frontier sweep found; warm-start differences could yield a slightly different optimum than the frontier row implies.

candidate_risks.concern: Ratio-constraint history is reconstructed by replaying the Lagrangian argmax in pure Python on the linearised DataFrame for each iteration's recorded lambdas, asserted to reproduce the Rust solver's per-iteration optimal_steps.
candidate_risks.why: The replay assumes the recorded lambdas are the pre-update lambdas used for that iteration's argmax and that the argmax is deterministic given lambdas+grid, with a special-cased final-iteration substitution for the non-converged averaged-lambda pass. Any drift between the Python replay's sign convention/precision (f32 vs f64) and the Rust argmax would silently mis-report history ratios. record_history is opt-in/off by default, limiting blast radius, but it is a genuine reimplementation-equivalence hazard.

candidate_risks.concern: _optimiser_service.py is ~5046 LOC and optimiser.py ~1803 LOC; a single module mixes pure helpers, artifact path/security validation, concurrency primitives, numerical-canonicalisation logic, and 4 large exception-handling orchestrators with heavily duplicated failure-mapping scaffolding.
candidate_risks.why: The two auto-range drivers, the solve setup driver, and the solver background all repeat ~10-arm exception->lifecycle-transition+metrics+cleanup blocks. Duplication of the terminal-reason mapping and orphan-cleanup logic is a maintenance and correctness hazard: a fix to one failure arm can easily be missed in the parallel copies, and the sheer size obscures the invariants. This is the explicit 'god-file architecture question' — strong candidate for extraction (artifact lifecycle, auto-range engine, ratebook factor-table serialisation, failure-mapping) into cohesive modules.

candidate_risks.concern: When frontier_enabled, the inline frontier compute in _finalize_solve_result catches ALL exceptions and records them only as a non-fatal result['frontier_error'] string while the solve still completes successfully.
candidate_risks.why: A genuine numerical/feasibility problem in the frontier (e.g. infeasible ranges, solver divergence, a real bug) is downgraded to a warning string the user may not notice, and the primary solve is reported as fully successful. This is broad-except error-swallowing on a numerical path; the project's stated philosophy prefers loud failure. Worth auditing whether frontier failures should at least surface as a distinct job warning state vs being buried in the result dict.

candidate_risks.concern: Server-owned artifact handles are validated against a temp-root and structural rules, but the validation relies on Path.resolve(strict=exists) and is_relative_to checks; handles are read back from the (in-memory) job dict and re-validated on every load/cleanup.
candidate_risks.why: The validation looks robust (absolute-path requirement, null-byte rejection, parent==root, prefix+filename checks). The residual lead is whether any path component could be a symlink created between persist and load that resolves outside root, or whether resolve(strict=False) on a non-existent path (used when the dir was already cleaned) could bypass the is_relative_to check. Lower priority given handles are server-generated (mkdtemp under a fixed root), not user-supplied, but the load/cleanup-from-job-dict pattern means a corrupted job dict is the trust boundary.

candidate_risks.concern: Estimate path deliberately does NOT run solve-grade NaN/inf value validation (only column presence, quote_id dtype, and null-quote_id), so estimate can report counts for data the subsequent solve will reject.
candidate_risks.why: Intentional cost trade-off (single scan) and documented, but it means the estimate and solve disagree on validity: a user sees a clean estimate then the solve fails on non-finite values. Not a correctness bug per se, but a UX/contract-divergence lead — and if any caller treats a successful estimate as a solvability guarantee, that assumption is unsound.

internal_dataflow: IN: HTTP request -> LocalTrustedHostMiddleware (host allowlist) -> LocalSessionMiddleware (Origin + x-haute-session-token for /api/*) -> _RequestIdMiddleware (bind request_id, time, catch->500) -> FastAPI router -> Pydantic body validation (schemas.py) -> route handler. Graph-bearing requests call flatten_graph(body.graph), _ensure_source_file (fills source_file from haute.toml), _validate_runtime_input_paths (resolve_runtime_file_path enforce_project_root). Sync/CPU-bound execution runs off-loop via run_in_threadpool / asyncio.to_thread / run_blocking_with_response_timeout. Preview/trace funnel through SupersessionCoordinator.run_latest (at most one running + one latest waiting per (operation, source_file, source, graph_fingerprint) key, bounded by an asyncio.Semaphore). Long jobs (train/solve/explore): handler validates, JobStore.create_job (status 'running'), spawns a daemon threading.Thread, returns {status:'started', job_id}; client polls GET .../status/{job_id}. Worker mutates job via JobStore.atomic_update (read-merge-swap under _write_lock; optional expected_status guard) and terminalises via JobLifecycle.transition (reason-precedence). Heavy runtime objects (solver/solve_result/quote_grid/factors_df) are kept in the job dict then stripped after heavy_object_ttl via threading.Timer or lazy sweep; the optimiser also spills apply/factor dataframes to temp-parquet artifacts behind validated handles (register_artifact_cleaner ties cleanup to job eviction). OUT: handler builds a schemas.py response model (FastAPI serialises to JSON; x-request-id echoed). Live sync OUT: file-watcher debounces (300ms) -> parses changed pipeline -> default_bus.publish('graph.update'|'parse.error', payload) -> server.py subscriber -> loop.create_task(broadcast(frame)) -> serialised per-socket send to every ws_clients member with a 1s hard send timeout.
concurrency_model: Hybrid asyncio + thread-pool + background daemon threads on a single uvicorn process (single-user trust model; multi-worker explicitly out of scope). Shared mutable singletons: (1) JobStore instances per prefix via @functools.cache get_job_store — all mutation linearises on a per-store threading.RLock (_write_lock); reads via get_job/has_job_* take the lock and run TTL eviction first; the .jobs property and a few optimiser sites read _jobs raw without the lock. (2) ws_clients set guarded by ws_clients_lock (threading.Lock) for add/discard/snapshot; broadcast iterates a snapshot and serialises concurrent sends per-socket via _ws_send_inflight/_ws_send_pending under _ws_send_state_lock. (3) default_bus EventBus uses a threading.RLock; publish snapshots the handler list and isolates handler exceptions. (4) _pipeline_index / _module_deps caches guarded by _pipeline_index_lock with double-checked locking + single-assignment publish; only startup and the file-watcher may invalidate. (5) self-write tracking (_self_write_paths) under _self_write_lock; save_lock (asyncio.Lock) serialises all save-shaped endpoints (pipeline/save, submodel/create, submodel/dissolve). (6) SupersessionCoordinator uses per-key asyncio.Condition + an asyncio.Lock over the state registry; CancellableJobRegistry / SingleFlightCoordinator use threading.RLock. (7) TrainService._start_lock + _check_no_concurrent_jobs enforces one running training job; optimiser allows estimate/auto-range concurrently with a solve. Cancellation is cooperative: ExecutionCancellationToken + threading.Event checked at worker checkpoints; Python cannot force-kill a worker thread, so response timeouts return 504 while the thread finishes in the background (run_blocking_with_response_timeout shields the task).
invariants: JobStore.atomic_update must replace the job dict by whole-dict swap under _write_lock so a concurrent reader sees either the old or new dict, never a half-merged one; two writers of disjoint keys must not lose each other's writes.
expected_status-guarded updates must skip (return None) when status no longer matches, so a timeout/supersession never overwrites a completed/terminal result.

JobLifecycle.transition reason-precedence (error<contract_error<memory_limited<cancelled<timed_out<superseded) must hold: a 'completed' terminal is final; lower-precedence reasons never replace a higher one.

get_job_store(prefix) returns exactly one JobStore per known prefix and distinct stores across prefixes, so a job_id minted under one prefix is never visible under another; direct JobStore() construction outside the factory is forbidden (pinned by tests/test_routes_hygiene.py).

Heavy runtime objects (solver/solve_result/quote_grid/factors_df/ratebook_factor_contexts) must be cleared after their short TTL while lightweight status/result metadata survives the full job TTL; artifact handles must be cleaned up exactly once when their owning job is evicted (register_artifact_cleaner).

Server-owned parquet artifact handles must resolve to absolute paths strictly inside the per-kind artifact root with the expected dir-prefix and filename (path-traversal/escape rejected by _validate_server_owned_parquet_handle).

validate_safe_path / resolve_runtime_file_path / _validate_runtime_input_paths must reject NUL bytes (400) and any path resolving outside the project root (403); the SPA static fallback must only serve files under STATIC_DIR (is_relative_to check).

schemas.py is the single backend<->frontend wire contract: the canonical graph types come from haute._types and are re-exported (not redefined); response models must not leak internal cache flags (e.g. _result_finite_validated is whitelisted out of TrainStatusResponse).

The event-bus WebSocket frame envelope must reserve the 'type' key (_ws_message_frame raises if payload already contains 'type'); subscribers must never let one handler's exception suppress delivery to others (EventBus.publish isolates).
The pipeline name->path index may be (re)built ONLY at startup and by the file-watcher; all other code treats it as read-only — two writers reintroduce a two-sources-of-truth race.
is_self_write must suppress file-watcher broadcasts for server-originated writes within the cooldown so save->reparse does not feed back into a broadcast loop.

validate_v2_schema must loud-fail (ApiInputSchemaError->422) on unknown column types (B1), filesystem-sanitised label collisions (B2), duplicate labels/column names, and malformed JSONPaths — never silently downgrade or clobber a parquet.
graph_fingerprint over (operation, source_file, source, graph) must uniquely key supersession so a stale preview/trace is cancelled and a newer same-key request supersedes it deterministically.
WebSocket /ws/sync and /api/* must require the local session token + local Origin unless HAUTE_DISABLE_LOCAL_SESSION_AUTH is set; token comparison must be constant-time (hmac.compare_digest).
perf_characteristics: Event loop is kept responsive by off-loading every CPU/IO-heavy operation to threads (run_in_threadpool / asyncio.to_thread / run_blocking_with_response_timeout). Preview/trace bounded by HAUTE_PREVIEW/TRACE_MAX_CONCURRENCY semaphores (default 2) and 120s response timeouts; supersession cancels superseded in-flight work so rapid graph edits don't pile up. Startup primes the pipeline index once (_ensure_pipeline_index) to avoid first-request discovery+parse of every pipeline; _clear_bytecache rglob over the source tree runs on every startup. File-watcher debounces 300ms and hashes raw file bytes before the expensive AST parse to skip byte-identical files; module edits only re-parse importing pipelines; config JSON edits re-parse all. JobStore eviction is O(n_jobs) on each create/get and runs under the write lock. Heavy optimiser/training dataframes are streamed to temp parquet (bounded_sink) and served lazily to cap peak RSS; completed-job heavy objects are dropped after 15min (active threading.Timer + lazy sweep). broadcast fan-out is O(clients) with a per-socket 1s send timeout and per-socket send serialisation (queued payloads coalesce). _optimiser_service.py is very large (~5046 lines) with deep streaming auto-range chunk-planning; estimate paths are contractually single-scan.

SupersessionCoordinator: per-key asyncio.Condition state machine with generation counters, limiter acquisition racing a superseded-wait, deferred limiter release tied to a background task's future, and reference-counted state teardown.

candidate_risks.concern: Optimiser background solve worker reads the live job dict lock-free via store.jobs.get(job_id, {}) (and store.jobs[job_id] in ~15 elapsed-seconds sites), bypassing JobStore._write_lock.
candidate_risks.why: The comment at _optimiser_service.py:2187 says this is deliberate to avoid _evict_stale() running from a background thread, but it reads _jobs concurrently with atomic_update's whole-dict swap and with eviction running on the polling thread. Whole-dict reference reads are atomic on CPython today, but on free-threaded 3.13 (which _helpers.py:319-324 explicitly anticipates for ws_clients) these become unsynchronised; and iterating .jobs elsewhere can race a dict resize. Silent-correctness/concurrency lead.

candidate_risks.concern: JobStore.jobs property returns the underlying _jobs dict by reference (no copy), and JobLifecycle.transition reaches into store.jobs[job_id] and store._write_lock directly (SLF001).
candidate_risks.why: Any caller that mutates or iterates the returned dict outside _write_lock can corrupt store state or observe a torn view during a concurrent swap/eviction. The lifecycle helper re-implements the locked merge by poking private members, so the JobStore invariant ('all mutation linearises on _write_lock') depends on every external caller's discipline rather than encapsulation.

candidate_risks.concern: EventBus typed payloads (GraphUpdatePayload, ParseErrorPayload) under-declare the runtime payload: the file-watcher publishes an extra 'graph_fingerprint' key not present in the TypedDicts.
candidate_risks.why: _event_bus.py:83-95 declares GraphUpdatePayload={graph, source_file} but server.py:644-651 publishes {graph, graph_fingerprint, source_file}; the @overload claims the typed shape while the impl widens to dict[str,Any], so type-checkers cannot catch a consumer that relies on the declared (incomplete) contract. Low-severity contract-drift lead — the WS frame correctly carries graph_fingerprint at runtime, but the typed bus contract is misleading.

candidate_risks.concern: broadcast() schedules sends as fire-and-forget loop.create_task from the event-bus subscriber (synchronous context inside the watcher's asyncio task); a frame can be dropped silently if no running loop exists.
candidate_risks.why: _broadcast_event_as_ws_message catches RuntimeError('no running loop') and logs+returns, dropping the graph_update for all clients. In production the watcher runs on the loop so this is fine, but any code path that publishes 'graph.update' off-loop (or during loop shutdown) loses the broadcast with only a debug log. The scheduled task's exceptions are only logged (fire-and-forget), so a persistent send failure surfaces only in logs. Reliability lead, not correctness.

candidate_risks.concern: SupersessionCoordinator deferred limiter/active-state release relies on exc.background_task being an asyncio.Future and uses asyncio.create_task inside done-callbacks; a tasked release that errors or a loop tear-down could strand a semaphore permit or leave state.active=True.
candidate_risks.why: The coordinator has multiple interacting failure branches (_acquire_limiter_unless_superseded, _clear_active_when_done, _release_limiter_when_done) that hand semaphore release to a background future's done-callback. If that future never completes (or completes after loop shutdown), the per-key Semaphore permit is not returned, eventually deadlocking that (graph,source) preview/trace key. Concurrency lead worth a focused audit + stress test under cancellation.

invariants: Sandbox containment: validate_user_code MUST reject every known CPython sandbox-escape vector (dunder attribute access, __builtins__ subscript, getattr/type/vars/super, frame/traceback walks, import/class/async/global/nonlocal) BEFORE exec(); safe_globals MUST strip __import__/open/eval/exec/compile/etc. The two layers are defence-in-depth — neither alone is sufficient.

Path containment: validate_project_path and validate_safe_path MUST resolve() first and reject any path not is_relative_to(project_root); resolution must never escape the sandbox root via .., symlinks, or embedded NUL bytes.

resolve_runtime_file_path with enforce_project_root=True (HTTP routes) MUST raise/return-None for absolute or relative paths escaping the project root; existing files win over missing candidates and prefer breaks ties deterministically.

Restricted unpickler: safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load MUST only construct globals whose (module,name) is in _ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES; single-segment prefixes match the package and dotted submodules but not lookalikes (numpy not numpy_evil).

Registry completeness: every NodeType MUST have BOTH an exec and a codegen builder (validate_registry_complete); duplicate registration MUST fail loudly; get_exec/get_codegen MUST raise (never silently fall back) on a missing entry so exec and codegen can never disagree.

Databricks cache safety: _cache_path_for MUST collapse a table name to one path component inside CACHE_DIR (reject traversal); fetch_and_cache MUST write to a unique temp file then atomically replace, and MUST raise FetchIntegrityError rather than cache when a retried batch lost rows (cursor.rownumber != rows_received) or a zero-row result carries no schema. SELECT clause MUST start with SELECT and contain no ;/--/ /* / dangerous keywords; table name MUST match catalog.schema.table.

Git guardrails: protected branches (main/master/develop/production, or HAUTE_PROTECTED_BRANCHES) MUST never be mutated; user-supplied refs/SHAs MUST pass _validate_ref_name (no leading '-', no control/glob/path chars) before reaching git CLI to prevent argument injection; destructive ops (revert/delete) MUST create + push a backup tag first; raw subprocess stderr MUST NOT reach HTTP (wrapped in GitError, sanitized) while authored messages use GitDomainError/GitGuardrailError.

Local session auth: real /api/* requests and websockets MUST present the per-process session token (hmac.compare_digest) and a trusted (loopback/configured) Origin, unless HAUTE_DISABLE_LOCAL_SESSION_AUTH is set; OPTIONS preflight is exempt.

Deploy test-before-live: deploy() MUST resolve -> validate_deploy (which scores every test quote and checks declared input schema + expected outputs) before dispatching; any structural or test-quote failure aborts with an aggregated DeployError. handle_deploy MUST block non-dry-run deploys outside CI.
Deploy reproducibility: container-based targets MUST use a patch- or digest-pinned base_image (validated at __post_init__ AND resolve_config); Dockerfile deps MUST be pinned to installed versions.

Deploy semantic preservation: the deployed scorer MUST reuse the dev execution engine and MUST verify the live input schema against the bundled feature contract at load time (assert_contracts_match); it MUST NOT manufacture predictions when a contract is bundled but the model artifact is absent (raises).

RAM guardrail conservatism: estimate_safe_training_rows returns no limit when source rows or column schema are unknown (None), and otherwise downsamples to >= _MIN_SAFE_ROWS so the estimate never silently trains on a dataset that won't fit; estimate is metadata-only (parquet footer), never executes the pipeline.

Bundler determinism: collect_artifacts MUST resolve every artifact path to an absolute path where the pipeline-relative file wins over CWD, and MUST raise (FileNotFoundError/DeployError) for missing artifacts or static-source schema drift rather than bundling a wrong file.

Impact correctness: percent-change math MUST refuse zero production baselines with non-zero staging (raises), MUST reject non-finite predictions, and MUST refuse truncated endpoint responses so the report never understates pricing impact.

candidate_risks.concern: Executor resolves pipeline-config file paths WITHOUT enforce_project_root, so a pipeline can read/scan files anywhere on the host filesystem at execution time
candidate_risks.why: execution.py:179 (canonical_dataframe_execution_graph) and execution.py:406 (_runtime_path_from_graph_config) call resolve_runtime_file_path(..., prefer='project') with enforce_project_root defaulting to False, unlike the HTTP routes which pass enforce_project_root=True. read_data_source/scan_parquet then open the resolved path. If pipeline graph JSON is ever attacker-influenced (e.g. an imported/shared pipeline, or a route that builds a graph from request data before the route-level path check), arbitrary-file read is possible. May be an intentional trust boundary (pipeline source is trusted code) but the asymmetry with the route layer is a sharp edge worth auditing.

candidate_risks.concern: _get_project_root() caches Path.cwd() at first call as a process-global; every path-containment check depends on it being correct
candidate_risks.why: _PROJECT_ROOT is lazily set to cwd at the time of the first _get_project_root() call (_sandbox.py:46-51). If any import-time or early code triggers resolution before the server has chdir'd to the real project, or if the server process cwd is broader than the intended root, validate_project_path/validate_safe_path silently authorize a wider tree. candidate_risks.concern: Atomic cache replace uses Path.replace across a temp file in the same dir, but read_cached_table/scan_parquet readers are not coordinated with concurrent fetch replace on Windows

On Windows, os.replace fails if the destination is open by a reader (scan_parquet holds the file). candidate_risks.why: fetch_was_retried gates the integrity check (_databricks_io.py:339,361-368). The reasoning is that only a failed-then-retried batch can have advanced cursor.rownumber. If the connector ever advances rownumber on a partially-consumed first batch that did NOT raise (driver quirk), rows could be dropped silently because the check is skipped. candidate_risks.concern: RAM/VRAM detection silently falls back to a fixed 4 GiB / None, and width estimation divides by row_count
candidate_risks.why: available_ram_bytes returns a hard 4 GiB on any failure (_ram_estimate.py:114-126) — on a small CI box or container with cgroup limits not reflected in /proc/meminfo MemAvailable, the estimate can be wildly off, causing either OOM (under-estimate of usage vs real cap) or needless downsampling. (2) HTTP requests -> _local_security middleware (token + Origin gate) -> routes -> _git operations / file reads via validate_safe_path. (4) Databricks: node http_path + env creds -> fetch_and_cache streams Arrow batches to local .haute_cache/<table>.parquet; runtime reads via read_cached_table -> scan_parquet. (5) Training: PipelineGraph + target node -> estimate_safe_training_rows reads ancestor parquet footers only.
